intro: Kandy's great tree stands just outside the city at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya: a weeping fig on the Great Lawn whose single crown shades somewhere between 1,600 and 2,500 square metres. It is more than a hundred years old, the gardens were formally established in 1843, and Peradeniya is about 20 minutes from Kandy by bus, tuk-tuk or train.
meta_description: The giant Java fig of Peradeniya's Great Lawn near Kandy, one tree shading up to 2,500 square metres: where it is and how to visit.
question_meta: Near Kandy, the Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya keep a giant Java fig whose crown shades up to 2,500 square metres.
question_answer: The tree to see near Kandy is the giant Java fig on the Great Lawn of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Peradeniya, about 6 kilometres west of the city. It is a weeping fig, Ficus benjamina, whose single crown has been measured at between 1,600 and 2,500 square metres, and it is more than a hundred years old.
question_context: The spread depends on who measured it: a 1988 encyclopedia piece gave about 1,600 square metres, a blogger about 2,420 and a Sunday Observer garden writer about 2,500. Its age is less certain than its size. Travel pieces say around 160 years and older writing a century, but no garden record of its planting has surfaced, so more than a hundred years is the safe statement. The gardens go back to groundwork in 1821 and were formally established in 1843 on 147 acres, and they are run by the Department of National Botanic Gardens. The fig was photographed on a colour slide in 1982, now in the University of Pennsylvania's library, and it is still the crown visitors on the lawn walk towards. Entry to the gardens is paid; the tree stands in the open, straight on from the main entrance. Peradeniya is around 20 minutes from Kandy by bus or tuk-tuk on the Peradeniya Road, or by train to Peradeniya Junction.

trees.story:
This is the same species people keep in a pot by the window, grown until one tree shades somewhere between 1,600 and 2,500 square metres of lawn. The figure depends on who did the measuring. A 1988 encyclopedia piece gave about 1,600, a blogger about 2,420, and a Sunday Observer garden writer about 2,500, describing it as a giant living umbrella.

It is a weeping fig, Ficus benjamina, known in Sri Lanka as the Java fig or Java willow, and it stands in the middle of the Great Lawn of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya, near Monument Road. The gardens themselves go back to groundwork in 1821 and were formally established in 1843, on 147 acres just outside Kandy.

Its own age is less certain than its size. Travel pieces put it at around 160 years, and older writing calls it a century old, but no garden record of when this tree went in has surfaced. More than a hundred years is the safe statement. If the Department of National Botanic Gardens has the planting date, we would like to hear it.

It has been a sight for a long time. Mary Binney Wheeler photographed it on a colour slide in 1982, now in the University of Pennsylvania's library, and it is still the crown everyone on the lawn walks towards.

Entry to the gardens is paid. Peradeniya is about 6 kilometres west of Kandy, around 20 minutes by bus or tuk-tuk, or by train to Peradeniya Junction.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one vast umbrella-shaped crown standing in the open in the middle of the Great Lawn. Walk straight on from the main entrance; it is near Monument Road.
